Article Title: $2 billion in secret accounts, UAE-Saudi dealings and more: What Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner's hacked phone allegedly revealed
Article Text:
Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner

Kushner calls allegations ‘fabrications’

US president Donald Trump’s son-in-law, Jared Kushner, has denied allegations linking him to secret foreign bank accounts and hundreds of millions of dollars in transfers. The claims involve alleged financial arrangements connected to Israel, the United Arab Emirates (UAE) and Saudi Arabia.According to Vanity Fair, Dutch investigators gained access to a Russian military intelligence-linked server through a Russian hacker who agreed to cooperate with British and Dutch authorities. The server contained screenshots of Kushner’s iPhone, allowing investigators to view his screen as he used it.The report alleged that Kushner accessed a UAE-linked bank account that received around $750 million through transfers routed via Azerbaijan. The account was held at First Abu Dhabi Bank and linked to the Watani Al Emarat Foundation, a UAE government-funded charity. Kushner was reportedly a signatory, although the account was not technically his.“Jared was looking for shortcuts in his diplomacy,” a source familiar with the alleged arrangement told Vanity Fair.The publication alleged that UAE President Mohamed bin Zayed and Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman initially discussed funding a foreign policy fund with Kushner during Donald Trump’s first administration.It said the broader proposal did not materialise as planned, but alleged that at least $2 billion was subsequently placed in two or more accounts.“Jared promised MBZ that he’d push their agenda with Trump if they participated in a fund. He wanted normalization with Israel so that business could take off,” the report said, quoting a source.Vanity Fair also alleged that around $1 billion was transferred to Israel via Azerbaijan into a separate account. It said some of the money may have been moved through Cyprus, while acknowledging that aspects of the alleged transactions remained unclear.Responding to the report, Kushner rejected the claims and challenged the author to produce evidence.“The allegations made by this author are completely insane and never happened,” he said.In a post on X, Kushner said, “No bank statements, wire transfer records, account numbers, transaction dates, or other verifiable details were provided to support these extraordinary accusations.”Kushner also said he had faced intense scrutiny, including congressional investigations and a special counsel investigation, and had voluntarily provided more than 30 hours of testimony.“None of these allegations ever surfaced, because none of these events ever happened,” he said.Calling the claims “outrageous fabrications”, he added, “This is not journalism. It is a mixture of fantasy, fiction, and advocacy, written by someone who is either deeply disturbed or acting with sinister intent.”Kushner’s counsel denied wrongdoing, while other individuals named in the report also disputed aspects of the allegations. The claims have not been established as proven wrongdoing. Any further assessment will depend on independently verifiable evidence, responses from those named and whether the allegations prompt formal scrutiny.
Article Summary: Kushner calls allegations ‘fabrications’ US president Donald Trump’s son-in-law, Jared Kushner, has denied allegations linking him to secret foreign bank accounts. The claims involve alleged financial arrangements connected to Israel, the United Arab Emirates (UAE) and Saudi Arabia.

Article Title: A three-year-old police Labrador whose arrival and training were funded by a $25,000 donation found a missing 70-year-old hiker in Hawaii Volcanoes National Park; it was her second successful rescue i
Article Text:
Trina, a Labrador from Sweden, had found a missing teenager in Waikoloa just a month earlier.

The rescue operation

Who is Trina, the police dog behind the rescue?

Missing hiker develops special connection with Trina

A 70-year-old man who went missing while hiking in Hawaii Volcanoes National Park was found by a three-year-old police Labrador named Trina on Monday. According to the Hawaii Police Department , authorities began searching for David Arai after he had not been seen for more than 24 hours. The dog eventually tracked him down about two miles from his rental vehicle, marking her second successful rescue in two months.Arai, who lives on Oahu, was familiar with the national park and frequently explored its trails. His son, Kaohe, told local television station KHON2 that his father often went hiking alone. This time, however, his absence led to a search involving police officers, national park personnel and a helicopter.By the time Trina found him at around 7.30 pm, the search had been under way for more than seven hours. Arai was lying slightly away from the trail, among bushes. He was subsequently carried to the trailhead and taken to Hilo Benioff Medical Center, where he received treatment for dehydration and exposure.Trina, a Labrador Retriever originally from Sweden, had helped locate an endangered teenager in Waikoloa, just a month earlier.Arai now hopes to adopt the dog if she ever retires from police service.The search began after Puna patrol officers received a report about Arai at 12.16 pm on Monday. According to the police, he had last been known to be in the Volcano area, and nobody had seen him for over a day.Investigators treated his disappearance as an endangered missing-person case after considering his age and information gathered during their investigation.An important development came when officers found Arai's rental vehicle inside Hawaii Volcanoes National Park, which helped establish an area for the search.Personnel from the police department and national park quickly began to search the surrounding area, while the Hawaii Fire Department deployed a helicopter to assist from above.Officer Christopher Ross, who works with the department's Area II Juvenile Aid Section and joined the operation with Trina, told KHON2 that the conditions along the trail were difficult. Recalling how he first spotted Arai, he said the man was lying on his back in bushes, a short distance away from the trail itself.“The conditions were pretty bad going down that trail. And the first thing I noticed, I saw the top of his head, and he was slightly off trail in the bushes, like pretty much lying on his back,” Ross said.The officer also described Trina's reaction when they reached the missing hiker. The Labrador not just simply stopped after finding him, but it approached Arai and licked his hand.“We led up to him, just wanted to make sure he was okay, and Trina, when she got next to him, she licked his hand basically to let him know that we found him and that he’s safe,” Ross said.Trina is trained as a live-find human tracking canine, a specialised police dog that helps locate missing people. She is also described as scent-discriminating, which means she can follow the scent of a particular individual.Her work with the Hawaii Police Department involves searches for missing children and endangered adults across Hawaii Island.Ross spoke warmly about his canine partner after Arai was found, describing how much her presence meant to him.“I don’t think there are any words to describe it. It’s a blessing just having this dog. It really is. Like my last thought, last before I fell asleep, was that we truly have an angel on our hands," he added.According to People magazine, Kaohe said his father was extremely grateful to the police department, park rangers and others who had participated in the operation. He was especially grateful to Ross and Trina, whose efforts ended the search.After meeting Trina, he also became interested in the possibility of giving her a home once her working years were over. “And if she ever retires and is looking for an adoption, he’s open. He said he fell in love with that dog,” Kaohe said.
Article Summary: David Arai, 70, went missing while hiking in Hawaii Volcanoes National Park on Monday. His disappearance led to a search involving police officers, national park personnel and a helicopter. Trina, a Labrador Retriever originally from Sweden, had helped locate an endangered teenager in Waikoloa just a month earlier.

Article Title: In 2020, Mississippi researchers applied blue pond dye 4 times to control algae in catfish ponds; musty fish still appeared in 2 treated ponds before harvest
Article Text:
AI-generated representative image showing blue pond dye being applied to a commercial aquaculture pond. Credits - Gemini

Where the

musty taste

comes from

What the researchers tried

Why the dye didn’t make it

AI-generated representative image showing clear groundwater emerging from a limestone opening and flowing into a woodland creek. Credits - Gemini

What farmers still rely on

Catfish aquaculture has a peculiar problem that most consumers never hear about. Processors taste a sample of the fish before harvesting; if the meat tastes musty or earthy, the pond is left unharvested until the taste goes away. A farmer with fish ready to sell has little to do but wait, and that can take days or weeks. The stakes are higher than they appear, because a customer who dislikes the flavour may not buy catfish again.One idea was to use pond dye. Some farmers wondered if the same approach might starve the algae responsible for the unpleasant flavour. A commercial blue dye called Aquashade is sold to control underwater weeds by reducing the amount of light that reaches them. Researchers from Mississippi tested the theory, and their results, published in January 2020 in the North American Journal of Aquaculture , were dismal. The colour did not stop the off flavour. In the study, fish that processors would have rejected as musty were found in two of three dyed ponds and two of three untreated ponds on the sample date just before harvest, so the dye made no difference.The taste comes from substances generated by blue-green algae. These are plant-like microorganisms that grow in warm, nutrient-rich ponds. The musty flavour is associated with a chemical called MIB, and the earthy flavour is associated with geosmin. The musty kind is almost invariably associated with one species, a filamentous-shaped alga known as Planktothrix perornata, which older literature refers to as Oscillatoria perornata, in the main catfish-growing area, the Mississippi Delta.Fish absorb these substances via their gills, skin and intestines, and the flavour develops in the flesh. Extension specialists say the taste can develop in minutes or hours, but it takes days or weeks to dissipate and longer for large, fatty fish in cold water. That slow purge is why farmers wanted a way to stop algal blooms before they started.The work was directed by Craig Tucker of the US Department of Agriculture’s research service and Charles Mischke of Mississippi State University, both at Stoneville. During the summer growth season, they applied Aquashade four times, at a concentration of roughly one part per million, once a month. The dye was applied to three channel catfish ponds, with three ponds as controls.Then the crew compared the ponds. The dye had no measurable effect on nitrite or ammonia levels, the number of extra hours of aeration required for the ponds, the amount of phytoplankton, which are the microscopic drifting plants and algae in the water, or fish production in the ponds. Algae known to produce smelly compounds turned up at some point in every pond, dyed or not. The more interesting question is why a dye that works on weeds had so little effect on this algae.The dye absorbs light in the orange and red part of the spectrum, at wavelengths of about 600 to 650 nanometres, reducing the light available to plants growing on the bottom. The blue-green algae that produce the smell are adapted to those low-light conditions. The researchers point to pigments other than chlorophyll and an ability to change position in the water, both of which help these species thrive in low light. They are therefore not much troubled by a dye that dims the pond. The study was limited, with three ponds in each group, so it did not answer all questions about pond dyes. But the result is clear enough for farmers to weigh their options. Shading the water neither prevented the off-flavour nor had any influence on fish productivity.A 1999 extension guide from the Southern Regional Aquaculture Center spells out the basic choices, and they are mostly practical ones. When the odour-producing species leave, the flavour disappears, so a farmer may simply wait, because algal blooms come and go. The most reliable method, it says, is to move the fish into clean water to purge the taste. The algae can also be eliminated with an approved algicide, although it warns that copper-based products are problematic because they can stress fish and deplete the pond of oxygen. Some of the products and rules it mentions may have changed since. More recent guidance from the Global Seafood Alliance likewise starts with taste-testing to identify the type of off-flavour.Farms also plan around the problem. Many keep fish of different sizes in each pond so that if one pond cannot be harvested because of off-flavour, then another is likely to hold fish which might be ready to sell. It is not an ideal strategy, the guide admits, but it keeps cash coming in. The Mississippi test shows that pond dye did not solve the off-flavour problem.
Article Summary: The taste comes from substances generated by blue-green algae. The musty flavour is associated with a chemical called MIB, and the earthy flavour with geosmin. A commercial blue dye called Aquashade is sold to control underwater weeds by reducing the amount of light that reaches them.

Article Title: In 2025, Wyoming’s Supreme Court rejected a landowner’s bid for a private road across his neighbour’s property; he wanted to reach a riverside meadow below a 60-foot drop
Article Text:
AI-generated representative image showing a steep rocky slope above a riverside meadow in Wyoming; the inset highlights a narrow trail descending the hillside. Credits - Gemini

The land and the drop

Why the private road failed

The easement claim

AI-generated representative image showing a grassy riverside meadow, a small horse corral and a steep hillside in a rugged Wyoming landscape. Credits - Gemini

What landowners can take from it

Roads, easements, and the goodwill of neighbours are the main sources of access in most places. Until someone wants to build, farm, or just walk to a beloved location, the gaps in that arrangement usually go unnoticed. When a dispute arises, courts must determine whether the need is real or merely a question of preference.Wyoming’s top court answered that question in 2025. On May 23, the Wyoming Supreme Court ruled against Samuel Tilden, who wanted a private road across his neighbour Linda Jackson’s land to reach a level meadow beside the South Fork of the Shoshone River, below a hillside with a 60-foot drop, or about 18 metres. The judges upheld two earlier Park County district court rulings. They said his land was not landlocked because a county road already ran through it, and that a steep slope on his own property was not the kind of problem the statute is meant to remedy.Tilden bought the property in 1996 and sold 23 acres, roughly 9 hectares, to Jackson and her late husband in 2010, keeping the area around it. He lived on a portion of what he retained until 2021, when he sold his house and the acreage to the west and south of Jackson’s property.He kept a final lot of 2.64 acres to the north. A county road ran straight through it on the steep hillside. Below it lay the river meadow, and the only way down was a very steep game trail that no car or ATV could use.Tilden testified that he retained the land so he could reach a favourite fishing spot. Before he divided up the property, he and his family had walked across what became Jackson’s land via a two-track road to the lower terrain to fish, skate on the ice, ride horses or walk the dogs. After the 2021 sale, he rented a cabin from Jackson and put a corral on the meadow, relocated six horses there and still used the same road to feed them.But January 2022 changed everything. Tilden planned to build a new cottage on the lower ground, so he moved out of the cabin he had been renting from Jackson. He offered to buy Jackson’s 23 acres, but she declined and told him she didn’t want him crossing her land anymore. He sued in June 2022, seeking the implied easement or a private road under Wyoming law.Wyoming’s constitution bars the taking of private land for private use without the owner’s consent, with one exception for private ways of necessity. A state law turns that exception into a process, but the applicant has to show the road is truly needed. In practice that means proving the land is landlocked, with no legally enforceable route to a public road, or that the existing route is so inconvenient that the difference amounts to necessity.Tilden could not pass the test. He admitted that the county road passed across his land and that he had a legal interest in the same, and he did not contend that the road in itself was very inconvenient. The actual grievance was that a natural barrier on his own property separated him from the lower level. That, the court said, was not the sort of necessity the law contemplates. The statute is meant to prevent landlocking, it stated, not to make a property easier to use or more valuable to sell.An implied easement can arise when one owner splits a property and, before the split, used a route across one part to serve the other. Three things must be shown. The land was once under common ownership and was later divided, the earlier use was apparent, obvious and continuous, and the route is necessary and beneficial to the land that relied on it.The trial judge looked at aerial images taken shortly after the separation and found no obvious trail from the county road over Jackson’s land to the meadow. The photos showed only a short loop around the well pump. A neighbour testified that he had never seen a way to the meadow, only a short track round the pump, and Jackson said she had assumed the track was for the well. The Supreme Court noted that it was more than ten years after the division of the property that Tilden first thought of building a cottage and corral below the drop. He also had not proved that he could not build on the 2.64 acres or continue using the game trail for fishing and other family activities.The decision is a reminder that access rights are best settled on paper at the moment land is divided. Anyone who sells part of a property while keeping another should work out how they will reach what remains and secure an easement in the sale documents, rather than relying on years of informal use. Without a written right, a neighbour’s goodwill can end, as it did here.For owners whose land really has no legal way out, Wyoming does offer a remedy. The constitutional exception for private ways of necessity and the state’s private road law have been explained by the Wyoming Supreme Court in earlier cases, including a 2007 ruling that traces the law back to 1895 and says damages are measured by comparing a property’s value before and after the road. That ruling notes that the original statute was amended in 2000, and the current procedure is set out in Wyoming Statute § 24-9-101. The constitutional wording it quotes also requires just compensation for any such taking.The other side of the coin is the Tilden case. A cliff, a game trail and a pleasant memory of fishing were not enough to compel a neighbour to give up a piece of her land. The court made it plain that the law protects those whose property would otherwise be useless and that seeking a better route to part of one’s own land is something else. Owners who want to develop in hard-to-reach corners of their property should check their access before they buy and ask for it in writing before they sell.
Article Summary: Samuel Tilden wanted a private road across his neighbour Linda Jackson’s land to reach a level meadow beside the South Fork of the Shoshone River, below a hillside with a 60-foot drop, or about 18 metres. The Wyoming Supreme Court ruled against him in 2025.

Article Title: In 2019, a tornado damaged a Texas couple’s home; State Farm paid nearly $293,000, but after a five-day trial, a jury and a 2025 appeals court rejected their claim that more was owed
Article Text:
AI-generated representative image showing a Texas-style suburban home with tornado-related roof damage beneath a cloudy sky; the inset highlights torn shingles and exposed roofing material. Credits - Gemini

From inspection to lawsuit

What the jury heard

AI-generated representative image showing roof-damage photographs, repair estimates and house keys beside a window overlooking a storm-damaged home under cloudy skies. Credits - Gemini

Why the appeal failed

A tornado can leave a family with two problems at once. Besides the damaged house itself, there is the repair estimate, which arrives later and is rarely in line with what the insurer is willing to pay. The gap between the two figures becomes the point of contention, because insurance covers insured losses rather than guaranteeing a home restored to the owner’s specifications. Few such disputes reach a jury; most end in settlement.Gary and Martha Smith, a couple from Texas, took theirs all the way. The Smiths held a homeowners policy with State Farm Lloyds, and in 2019 a tornado hit their property. State Farm paid them $292,901.67 for covered losses and additional living expenses, but the Smiths felt they deserved considerably more. After a five-day trial, a jury sided with the insurer, and on December 2, 2025, the Fifth Circuit , a US federal appeals court, affirmed the verdict in an unpublished opinion.After the tornado, the insurer sent an inspector to assess the damage. The Smiths were not happy with the assessment and claimed that the company had acted in bad faith, a term that often refers to an insurer arbitrarily withholding money it owes. They wanted $2.5 million before any lawsuit was filed. They sued in the US District Court for the Eastern District of Texas, alleging breach of contract and violations of Texas insurance law.By closing argument, the sum they were asking for had grown to somewhere between $25 million and $250 million. The Smiths said that award should send a message to the insurer. The jury then weighed five days of evidence before reaching its verdict.The trial lasted for five days and included eight witnesses, 36 factual stipulations, or facts the two parties agreed to in advance, and 384 exhibits. Experts were called in from both sides, but they disagreed fiercely on the extent of the damage. The insurer’s engineer, Joe Shahid, testified that the house could be restored to its pre-tornado condition with minimal modifications. Another expert for the insurer, Gary Boyd, who specialises in construction methods and repair costs, said the Smiths’ estimates were inflated and indicated a full remodel rather than necessary repairs.The Smiths’ own experts disagreed, but a jury is entitled to believe the evidence of one party. The jury found that the insurer had not breached its policy, had not engaged in any unfair or deceptive behaviour and had not failed to pay the whole claim. The appeals court added that the insurer had prepared its own estimate of the damage, shared it with the couple and even offered to resolve any differences in repair costs. The couple’s appeal focused on a procedural misstep by the insurer rather than on the size of the claim.The stumbling block was photographs. Shahid had taken 993 photos of the property and relied on them in part for his report, but the insurer did not turn them over until the eve of trial. That was a breach of the court’s scheduling order and restrictions on disclosure of expert material. The Smiths requested the judge to strike Shahid in its entirety. Instead, the court limited his evidence to the images that had been shared on time, excluded the late ones, struck any mention of them and kept them out of the jury chamber.The appeals court approved their selections. Shahid had been deposed by the Smiths before and they knew his views; therefore, there was nothing surprising about his testimony, it said. The pictures also mostly used images they had already received. The couple had multiple opportunities to ask for a mistrial and at one point rejected the judge’s offer to declare one. The court held that since they had accepted the judge’s directions at the time, they could not dispute the verdict on the same grounds later on.Appeals courts are reluctant to overturn jury verdicts. The Fifth Circuit emphasised the role of the jury, not the judge, in weighing evidence and deciding which witnesses to believe. The verdict is sufficient as long as there is competent evidence in the record to support it. The trial court had also refused to grant a new trial, judging the jury's findings to be sound.But homeowners who believe an offer is too low do have options before a case hits the courtroom. The Texas Department of Insurance proposes submitting documentation, like a contractor’s estimate, to explain the dispute to the insurer, using the policy’s appraisal procedure if available, or filing a complaint with the department. If those measures fail, mediation and litigation remain options.The case of the Smiths is an example of the power of a jury’s judgment when the evidence is presented. The ruling was not published and, as such, is not binding on other courts, but it shows how far a bad faith claim can travel and how a payment of nearly $293,000 can still become the centrepiece of a five-day trial.
Article Summary: Gary and Martha Smith, a couple from Texas, took theirs all the way. State Farm paid them $292,901.67 for covered losses and additional living expenses, but the Smiths felt they deserved considerably more. After a five-day trial, a jury sided with the insurer, and on December 2, 2025, a US federal appeals court, affirmed the verdict in an unpublished opinion.

Article Title: In 2021, more than 9 inches of rain poured over a Mississippi home; State Farm refused to pay about $16,000 for a full roof replacement, but a 2025 appeals court reversed the dismissal and sent the ca
Article Text:
AI-generated representative image showing a house during heavy rain, with the inset highlighting water leaking through a damaged ceiling. Credits - Gemini

The storm and the roof

Who must prove what

AI-generated representative image showing rainwater dripping through a ceiling inside a home, illustrating the roof-leak dispute. Credits - Gemini

What happens next

Few insurance disputes are as familiar as the one that follows a heavy downpour. When rain gets into a house, the roof is blamed, but the homeowner and the insurer often cannot agree on the cause. Who pays depends on whether the roof was already in poor condition or was damaged by the storm. Behind that sits a bigger question: who must prove what.That question ended up in federal court after a storm passed through Greenwood, Mississippi, in June 2021. Rain streamed into their house, and Mark and Margie Barger asked State Farm to pay for a brand new roof. The insurer disputed about $16,000 of the claim, and a lower court agreed. But in March 2025, the Fifth Circuit , the US federal appeals court covering Mississippi, Louisiana and Texas, overturned the ruling on the burden of proof, vacated the dismissal and sent the case back to the lower court.It was a bad storm. Almost 8 inches of rain fell on June 10 alone, and the storm total came to about 9.25 inches, or roughly 23.5 cm, according to the Fifth Circuit’s opinion. Water poured through the roof and ceilings of the Bargers’ single-storey house in at least seven places, and all three bedrooms, the dining and living rooms, a hallway and the foyer were affected.The couple said their eleven-year-old roof had never leaked before that night and kept leaking afterwards.The insurer paid for the interior damage and the couple’s belongings but would not pay for a new roof. Its position was that the only covered roof damage came from nine wind-damaged shingles and a small patch of roofing membrane. In plain terms, the insurer accepted that the storm had done some harm, just not enough to justify a new roof. The Bargers paid for a replacement themselves in March 2022 and sued for breach of contract two months later. The amount still in dispute was $16,023.79, plus an extra $3,120 to $5,000 in higher material costs.The district court granted summary judgment to State Farm, resolving the dispute without trial. The rationale was that the policy covered wind and hail, but not wear, decay or latent faults, and that the Bargers had not shown evidence indicating a covered event caused the additional damage. It also found that the only expert testimony as to cause pointed to faults in the construction.The problem, the appeals judges found, was that the district court had applied the wrong burden of proof. It had relied on the policy wording for personal property, which lists specific risks such as windstorm or hail, instead of the wording for the dwelling itself. Dwelling coverage is different. Insurers call this all-risk protection, which covers accidental direct physical loss unless an exception applies.That disparity changes the burden of proof under Mississippi law, the state Supreme Court said in a 2009 case, Corban v. USAA. Simply put, the question is who has the burden of proof to establish why the water got in. With all-risk coverage, the homeowner only has to prove that a physical loss occurred. After that, it is up to the insurer to prove that an exclusion such as wear and tear accounts for it. With a named-perils policy, the burden shifts and it is the policyholder who must prove that the harm was caused by a covered hazard. The trial court misstated the test, and thereby imposed an additional and more onerous duty on the Bargers.State Farm contended that the mistake was a clerical error that didn’t matter. The appeals court wasn’t persuaded and wrote that water had spilt into seven separate portions of the property, enough to create a genuine issue of material fact as to whether the roof system sustained accidental physical loss in the storm.The appeals court did not order any payment to the Bargers. In particular, it declined to opine on whether either side had met its burden on the policy exclusions, such as wear and tear or structural faults, leaving that to the district court when the case returns to it. The insurer may still argue the damage was caused by the way the roof was built or by wear. The difference now is that the insurer must prove an exclusion applies.Policyholders who think a claim has been mishandled can contact their state regulator. The Mississippi Insurance Department accepts complaints online and sends a copy to the insurer. It asks for supporting paperwork such as a denial letter and a copy of the policy within two working days and says it cannot aid anyone already represented by a lawyer or who needs legal guidance.Keeping dated photos of leaks, storm data, and proof of the roof’s prior condition gives a claim something concrete to rest on, regardless of who bears the burden. The insurer’s argument that only a tiny portion of the roof was storm damaged has yet to be tested at trial. The ruling was not published, so it is not binding on other courts.
Article Summary: Mark and Margie Barger asked State Farm to pay for a brand new roof. The insurer disputed about $16,000 of the claim, and a lower court agreed. But in March 2025, the Fifth Circuit overturned the ruling on the burden of proof.

Article Title: In 2022, a Texas couple found their vacant rental house stripped of its air conditioner, copper wiring and plumbing; Allstate denied the claim, and a 2025 appeals court upheld the ruling for the insur
Article Text:
AI-generated representative image showing a vacant rental house with its outdoor AC unit missing; the inset shows disconnected copper plumbing. Credits - Gemini

What the policy covered

How the case came together

AI-generated representative image showing disconnected copper plumbing and removed fixtures inside a vacant rental house. Credits - Gemini

Vacant vs. unoccupied

On paper, buying a home to rent out is straightforward: find a tenant, fix up the property and start collecting rent. The insurance policy normally sits in a drawer until something goes wrong. At that point, owners often discover that rental property coverage comes with restrictions on how the building is used. Insuring a home with no occupants differs greatly from insuring one with occupants, and the difference can be costly.That is what one Texas couple found in 2022. In 2021, Bradley and Crystal Childers bought an investment property in Lufkin, insured it with Allstate Indemnity Company and began renovations while looking for a tenant. In March 2022, the house was stripped of its air conditioning equipment, copper wiring and plumbing. The insurer rejected the claim, and in February 2025 the Fifth Circuit , a US federal appeals court, upheld a finding in its favour. The key question was whether the residence had been vacant for more than 60 consecutive days before the theft, a dispute that turned on the meaning of two everyday terms.The Childerses held what Allstate called a Landlords Package Policy, and two of its provisions mattered, according to the Fifth Circuit’s opinion. One covered damage to the exterior of a structure caused by a burglar breaking in, but only if the house was complete and had not been vacant or unoccupied for more than 60 consecutive days before the loss.The other covered fire damage caused by vandalism, with the same 60-day condition. Both protections would disappear if a property sat vacant or unoccupied long enough.Bradley’s grandparents drove past on 29 March 2022 and saw that the pad for a new air conditioning unit had been stripped. The couple rushed over and found the house burgled and vandalised. Police lifted a fingerprint, but nobody was ever identified. Crystal later testified that Allstate first told her the policy would pay but a few days later said the claim was refused because it believed the property had been vacant or unoccupied for more than 60 consecutive days. The couple sued in Texas state court, and the insurer moved the case to federal court.After the dispute began, the insurer sent written requests asking the couple to confirm a few basic facts, such as whether they had lived at the house, whether it was inhabited, and whether a tenant had ever stayed there. The Childerses never responded. Under federal court rules, requests left unanswered are treated as admitted, and the judge accepted the statements as true.Later, when the insurer asked for summary judgment, a ruling without a full trial when the key facts are not genuinely in dispute, Crystal filed an affidavit describing the Lufkin house as the couple’s home and saying they lived there. That conflicted with her earlier sworn testimony. In her deposition, she had said the house was bought as a rental, that the couple had lived in Wells, Texas, for six years, and that nobody had lived at the Lufkin property since the purchase. The trial judge struck the affidavit paragraph as a sham, meaning a later statement that contradicts earlier sworn evidence without explanation, and the appeals court said that was within the judge’s discretion.The couple argued that Lufkin was a secondary residence and the policy was ambiguous on the matter. The court was not convinced. It was a landlord's insurance, it said, which presupposes that the owners reside someplace else. Its description of the insured premises specified the building at the stated address rather than the owners’ personal house.Under Texas law , the two terms are not the same. A property is vacant when it has no furnishings of any real use, so a house with furniture is not vacant. The Lufkin property still had vanities, dressers and mirrors inside, so the insurer could not win on the vacancy argument alone.But occupancy is about people, not belongings. A house is occupied when people regularly use it as a place to live, and it is unoccupied when they do not. Furniture does not change that. The exclusion applied to properties that were vacant or unoccupied, and Crystal’s own testimony indicated that nobody had lived in the house for at least 60 days before the loss, so one word was sufficient. A federal court cannot redefine a term contrary to what the Texas Supreme Court has previously said.Owners who disagree with an insurer’s assessment have options. The Texas Department of Insurance recommends that policyholders explain to the company why they disagree and supply supporting documents such as a contractor’s estimate. If that does not work, many policies provide an appraisal procedure, and policyholders can also file a complaint with the department, request mediation, or go to court. That advice is meant for homeowners and renters, so landlords should review their own policy’s handling of disputes.The case hinged on facts the couple could not change by the time it reached court. The appeals court did not designate its opinion for publication, which typically means it is not binding precedent. Nevertheless, it shows how Texas courts interpret these terms and how quickly a 60-day gap can decide a claim.
Article Summary: Bradley and Crystal Childers bought an investment property in Lufkin, Texas, in 2021. They insured it with Allstate Indemnity Company and began renovations while looking for a tenant. In March 2022, the house was stripped of its air conditioning equipment, copper wiring and plumbing. The key question was whether the residence had been vacant for more than 60 consecutive days before the theft, a dispute that turned on the meaning of two everyday terms.

Article Title: In 2010, Paul Walker started a disaster-relief group after the Haiti earthquake; more than a decade after the actor's death, the organisation's volunteers helped 13,093 people in 2025 alone
Article Text:
Paul Walker founded a Haiti relief group in 2010; it helped 13,093 people in 2025 (Image Credit: Reach Out WorldWide)

How the Haiti earthquake inspired Paul Walker

How ROWW responds when disaster strikes

From Haiti to disaster zones around the world

What the 2025 figures reveal

More than a decade after actor Paul Walker died, the disaster-relief organisation he founded continues to help communities affected by natural disasters. Reach Out WorldWide (ROWW), established in 2010 following the devastating earthquake in Haiti, reported that it impacted 13,093 people through its work in 2025, supported by 738 volunteers. According to the organisation’s official Our Impact page, its work focuses on filling gaps in emergency response, particularly when affected communities need immediate assistance before larger relief operations are fully mobilised. The latest figures reflect how Walker’s original effort has grown into a continuing disaster-response mission.Walker, best known for his role in The Fast and the Furious film franchise, founded ROWW after travelling to Haiti in January 2010, following a powerful earthquake that devastated the country. He assembled a team of friends and volunteers to provide assistance to people affected by the disaster. During the response, Walker recognised that communities needed more than donated supplies. Skilled volunteers, including medical professionals and people with construction experience, could help address urgent needs that might otherwise go unmet.After returning from Haiti, he established ROWW to organise similar responses to natural disasters.The organisation’s mission was built around deploying small, agile teams that could reach affected areas quickly and work alongside local responders. Walker participated in relief efforts himself rather than limiting his involvement to fundraising. His commitment helped establish the organisation’s hands-on approach, which continues to guide its work.ROWW describes its work as filling the gap between a disaster and the arrival of wider assistance. Its teams include volunteer first responders and professionals with medical and construction expertise, allowing them to support local communities during the early stages of recovery. The organisation's work extends beyond immediate relief, with volunteers helping communities address urgent needs after disasters.Medical volunteers, including nurses and paramedics, provide care when local healthcare facilities are overwhelmed or difficult to reach. The organisation also distributes essential supplies and supports rebuilding work, depending on the needs of each affected community. ROWW says its smaller teams allow it to mobilise quickly and reach places that may receive limited attention from larger relief organisations. Its assistance is provided at no cost to disaster survivors, helping families preserve their resources for longer-term recovery.The organisation's work expanded beyond its initial response in Haiti. Its official impact page records deployments to Chile in 2010, the Philippines in 2011, Nepal in 2014, Vanuatu in 2015, Fiji in 2016, Indonesia in 2018 and the Bahamas in 2019. It also responded during the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020 and assisted communities in Oregon and Tennessee in 2021. In 2023, its deployment history included Turkey, followed by North Carolina in 2024 and California and Jamaica in 2025.These responses demonstrate how the organisation's original mission has developed to address different emergencies, from earthquakes and hurricanes to floods and other disasters. The specific work varies according to local conditions, with teams providing practical support where it is most urgently needed.ROWW's official impact page reports that 13,093 people were impacted by its work in 2025, with 738 volunteers contributing during the year. These figures offer a measure of the reach of a programme that relies heavily on volunteer participation. The organisation also publishes annual impact reports and financial disclosures, allowing supporters to examine its activities and funding. Its approach places emphasis on practical assistance, rapid deployment and cooperation with local communities rather than measuring relief solely through money spent or supplies distributed.Walker died in a car crash in November 2013, aged 40. His disaster-relief initiative has continued through the organisation he established, with volunteers carrying forward its focus on helping communities recover after emergencies. The 2025 figures show how the effort that began with a small relief team responding to the Haiti earthquake has developed into a continuing operation. For ROWW, the central aim remains to reach people facing urgent needs, restore access and safety, and provide support during the difficult period between a disaster and long-term recovery.
Article Summary: Reach Out WorldWide (ROWW) was established in 2010 following the Haiti earthquake. It reported that it impacted 13,093 people through its work in 2025, supported by 738 volunteers. Its work focuses on filling gaps in emergency response, particularly when affected communities need immediate assistance.

Article Title: In 1954, an Alabama farmer found a piece of a meteorite on a dirt road; he sold it for enough to buy a farm and a car, but the exact price was never reported
Article Text:
AI Representation: An Alabama farmer discovered a meteorite on a dirt road and sold it for enough money to buy a house and a car. Image credits: Chatgpt

The Hodges stone and the fireball over Oak Grove

Julius Kempis McKinney

and the second stone

The Hodges meteorite, the Sylacauga stone that struck Ann Hodges in Alabama. Image credits: Wikimedia Commons

A sale to the Smithsonian whose price was never reported

What a 2019 NASA analysis says about meteorite strikes on people and buildings

The fall, recovery, classification, and initial characterization of the Hamburg, Michigan

H4 chondrite

Why the two Sylacauga stones ended so differently

Most stony meteorites give little warning beyond a bright fireball and a series of sonic booms. In the following minutes, questions will start arising about what landed and where. Once such a meteoroid starts breaking down in the upper atmosphere, the resulting chunks do not stay together and scatter all around, landing on rooftops, in fields and even in the middle of the road. It all depends on the finder and their ability to determine the significance of the find. Such instances were recorded twice in the famous fall in the Southern United States and it is also the same case where there is not a single piece of financial information revealed.The Encyclopedia of Alabama records that a meteorite crashed through the roof of a home near Sylacauga, in Talladega County, on November 30, 1954 and struck resident Ann E. Hodges. The rock reportedly weighed about eight and a half pounds and is now on display at the Alabama Museum of Natural History in Tuscaloosa. The minerals database Mindat suggests that the rock first hit a radio console and then struck Mrs.Hodges. Mindat gives the stone’s weight as 3.86 kilograms, while the combined weight of the two stones is reported as 5.54 kilograms. It categorizes it as a chondrite of the H4 type. Mindat lists the fall time as 12:46 hours on November 30, 1954. The ownership of the meteorite was a point of conflict as well. While the encyclopedia claims that it was only after the intervention of the congressman, Kenneth Roberts, that the stone was returned to the state, Alabama Living magazine claims that the landlady of the Hodges returned it to the Hodges family in 1955 for $500.The second stone was discovered by Julius Kempis McKinney, a local farmer who, the Encyclopedia of Alabama says, found it on a dirt road on December 1, 1954, when his mules refused to move because of the black rock. He sold the piece through a lawyer and it went to the Smithsonian Institution, for enough money to buy a small farm and a used car.There are different stories of the discovery. One of them says that he brought the stone to the postman, who was the only government representative he trusted. Another story states that he put the stone aside and came back home in the evening, having heard about the stone of the Hodges. Mindat lists the McKinney stone’s weight as 1.68 kilograms. The postman and McKinney concluded that there must be a connection between the rock and the Hodges stone and it could be valuable. The information can be found on the Weekly Recess website.Alabama Living reports that the sum was never revealed and the Weekly Recess and Bizzarro Bazar websites likewise give no figure for the amount. The Encyclopedia of Alabama describes McKinney as probably the only major figure in the story to claim a satisfactory ending. Smithsonian magazine reports that McKinney’s stone is in the collections of the Smithsonian’s National Museum of Natural History, where it is on view. Hodges donated her stone to the Alabama Museum of Natural History in 1956, after the ownership dispute left her unable to find a buyer, according to Sky at Night Magazine.The NASA analysis, Kinetic Damage from Meteorites , presented as a poster at the 2019 Planetary Defense Conference, describes the Sylacauga stone as a 4-kilogram meteorite that indirectly hit Hodges. In addition, a 4-gram stone falling onto a young boy is recorded for the 1992 Mbale fall; neither incident caused death. The poster adds that fragments on the order of 0.1 kilograms may be enough to cause serious human injury or death and it cites Halliday et al.’s 1985 estimate that a person is struck by a meteorite roughly once a decade, most likely by a gram-sized piece. A second study,, published in Meteoritics & Planetary Science , examined a stone from the 2018 Michigan fall that belongs to the same H4 group as the Sylacauga stones.The same NASA poster also lists 48 meteorites found in North America between 1962 and 2016, of which 23 fell on roofs or buildings and three on cars. In other words, a meteorite striking a building is not unusual, but one striking a person, as happened to Hodges, remains extremely rare. McKinney’s good fortune lay in recognizing that the rock might be valuable and acting on it.
